theory.intro: A **continuous random variable** is measured rather than counted, so it can take any value in an interval. Because an interval holds infinitely many values, the probability of any one exact value is $0$.
facts: A continuous random variable comes from measuring something such as a length, time, mass, temperature or speed.
Its possible values fill an interval such as $0 < x < 100$, so they cannot be listed one by one.
Rounding a measurement to the nearest unit does not make the variable discrete, because the quantity measured still varies continuously.
$P(X = a) = 0$ for every single value $a$, since one point has no width on the number line.
So probability is only meaningful over an interval, written $P(a < X < b)$.
Because the endpoints contribute nothing, $P(a < X < b) = P(a \le X \le b) = P(a \le X < b) = P(a < X \le b)$.
For the same reason $P(X < c) = P(X \le c)$ and $P(X > c) = P(X \ge c)$.
The complement rule still holds, so $P(X > c) = 1 - P(X \le c)$.

foundation.question_text: Let $T$ be the time, in seconds, a swimmer takes to complete $100$ m. State whether $T$ is discrete or continuous, and give a reason.
foundation.solution_text:
Time is measured, not counted.
Any value in an interval such as $50 < t < 70$ is possible.
$T$ is continuous.

foundation.question_text: Let $N$ be the number of text messages a person sends in a day. State whether $N$ is discrete or continuous, and give a reason.
foundation.solution_text:
Messages are counted, not measured.
The possible values are the separate steps $0, 1, 2, \dots$
$N$ is discrete.

foundation.question_text: The mass of a bag of flour is recorded to the nearest gram. Let $M$ be that mass. State whether $M$ is discrete or continuous, and give a reason.
foundation.solution_text:
Mass is measured, so the true mass can be any value in an interval.
Recording it to the nearest gram rounds the record, not the quantity.
$M$ is continuous.

foundation.question_text: A quiz is marked out of $20$ and $S$ is the mark scored. State whether $S$ is discrete or continuous, and give a reason.
foundation.solution_text:
The mark is a count of correct answers.
The possible values are the whole numbers from $0$ to $20$.
$S$ is discrete.

foundation.question_text: The lifetime $L$, in hours, of a battery is a continuous random variable. Write down $P(L = 24)$.
foundation.solution_text:
$L$ is continuous, so every single value has probability $0$.
$P(L = 24) = 0$

foundation.question_text: A continuous random variable $X$ has $P(2 < X < 6) = 0.41$. Find $P(2 \le X \le 6)$.
A continuous random variable $X$ has $P(X \le 9) = 0.73$. Find $P(X < 9)$.

development.question_text: A continuous random variable $X$ has $P(X \le 12) = 0.28$. Find $P(X > 12)$.
The waiting time $W$, in minutes, for a bus is a continuous random variable. Explain why $P(W = 4.5) = 0$.
development.solution_text:
Probability is the area under the density curve of $W$.
The value $4.5$ is a single point, so the strip above it has zero width.
A region of zero width has zero area, so $P(W = 4.5) = 0$.

development.question_text: A continuous random variable $X$ has $P(X \ge 5) = 0.34$. Find $P(X > 5)$.

development.solution_text:
$X$ is continuous, so the region above the single value $2.5$ has zero width.
$P(X = 2.5) = 0$

development.question_text: A continuous random variable $X$ has $P(1 \le X \le 4) = 0.55$ and $P(X < 1) = 0.18$. Find $P(X > 4)$.
A machine records the volume $V$, in litres, of milk in a carton, correct to two decimal places. State whether $V$ is discrete or continuous, and justify your answer.
development.solution_text:
Volume is measured, so the true volume can be any value in an interval.
Rounding to two decimal places only limits how the value is written down.
$V$ is continuous.

mastery.question_text: A continuous random variable $X$ has $P(X < 7) = 0.36$ and $P(X > 11) = 0.22$. Find $P(7 \le X \le 11)$, and state whether $P(7 < X < 11)$ has a different value.
Explain why $P(X \le 6)$ and $P(X < 6)$ must be equal when $X$ is continuous, even though they can differ when $X$ is discrete.
mastery.solution_text:
$P(X \le 6) = P(X < 6) + P(X = 6)$ for any random variable.
For a continuous variable $P(X = 6) = 0$, so the two probabilities are equal.
For a discrete variable $P(X = 6)$ can be positive, so the two probabilities can differ.
